title: Consoltex Inc. (Mar 1997 TCC) Tax Court Canada Ruling
subject: Textile manufacturer SR&ED appeal examining whether fabric dyeing and weaving process improvements qualified for credits.
outcome: Appeal allowed in part; court found certain systematic textile experiments qualified as SR&ED while routine trials did not.
summary: Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen (1997 TCC) is a Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for Canadian manufacturers conducting shop-floor experimental production. Judge Bowman held that selling experimental output does not reduce eligible expenditures under section 37 of the Income Tax Act, rejected netting and carve-out formulas, and found the audit settlement agreement non-binding.
metaDescription: Review the landmark March 1997 Tax Court of Canada SR&ED decision for Consoltex Inc. on Canadian R&D tax credit evidence.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen (Docket: 94-990(IT)G, rendered March 4, 1997, reported at 97 D.T.C. 724 and [1997] 2 C.T.C. 2846) stands as a foundational authority in Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development ("SR&ED") tax jurisprudence. Presided over by the Honourable Judge Donald G.H. Bowman, the appeal addressed two critical intersections of tax administration and industrial research: first, whether an audit-level compromise settlement executed between a corporate officer and a Department of National Revenue ("DNR", now the Canada Revenue Agency or "CRA") assessor legally bars a taxpayer from appealing subsequent reassessments; and second, whether expenditures incurred during shop-floor experimental production—specifically high-volume raw material costs—must be reduced via "netting" or "carve-out" formulas when the resulting experimental goods are subsequently sold on the commercial market.
Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's Claim

Consoltex Inc. ("Consoltex"), a major Canadian textile manufacturer headquartered in Ville St-Laurent, Quebec, operated woven fabric manufacturing and converting facilities structured across four commercial divisions: fashion, outerwear, industrial, and print. During its taxation years ending December 31, 1985, December 31, 1986, June 30, 1987, December 31, 1987, and December 31, 1988, Consoltex claimed current SR&ED expenditures pursuant to subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada) (the "Act") and corresponding Investment Tax Credits ("ITCs") pursuant to subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Act.

Unlike pure research institutions operating isolated laboratory facilities, Consoltex conducted its experimental development directly on the plant floor using its commercial weaving looms and dyeing and finishing equipment. In the textile industry, translating fibre and chemical concepts into functional fabrics requires navigating complex, interacting physical and chemical variables across two primary operational stages: the weaving stage and the converting stage. The weaving stage encompasses beaming or warping, which involves winding hundreds or thousands of parallel yarns onto a cylindrical warp beam under precise tension; slashing or sizing, which entails immersing yarns in specialized polymer and chemical baths to coat the fibres and protect them against mechanical abrasion and breakage during high-speed weaving; entering, where individual warp yarns are threaded through heddle frame guides on the loom that move in sequence to create a gap or shed; and weaving itself, where filling yarns are interlaced across the warp shed via traditional shuttles, projectiles, rapiers, or high-velocity water and air jets. Once the greige fabric is woven, it transitions to the converting stage, which comprises preparation (chemical removal of the protective sizing polymers applied prior to weaving), dyeing (subjecting the fabric to complex chemical dye formulations through specialized thermal and chemical techniques), and finishing (applying mechanical, chemical, or thermal treatments to impart targeted performance properties such as flame retardancy, ballistic resistance, breathability, or surface lustre).

Because of the continuous, high-speed nature of industrial looms and converting ranges, resolving technological uncertainties in yarn behaviour, sizing chemistry, loom kinematics, or dye uptake frequently required weaving and processing thousands of metres of fabric across multiple experimental trials. Consequently, raw material outlays—principally the cost of yarn—far exceeded the cost of labour and overhead, at least in the fashion and outerwear divisions: for 1988, raw materials cost $534,542 against $287,453 of labour and overhead in the fashion division, and $806,168 against $278,574 in the outerwear division; Judge Bowman surmised that similar proportions existed in the other divisions, although this was not in evidence. Following the completion of these experimental runs, Consoltex routinely sold the resulting fabrics on the open market—including first-quality experimental yardage as well as substandard or technically failed batches sold as "seconds" or repurposed for alternative applications—in some cases for proceeds exceeding the cost of the related SR&ED expenditures; indeed, Judge Bowman found that probably the larger part of the fabrics produced in the course of the SR&ED was sold and that the total proceeds of such sales exceeded the SR&ED expenses claimed.

For the 1988 taxation year, Schedule I audit calculations reflected slightly adjusted allowed SR&ED expenditures of $1,103,788 and allowed ITCs of $220,758. Two unrelated non-SR&ED issues raised in the initial Notice of Appeal (a 1982 non-capital loss deduction and a $1,118,730 undepreciated capital cost opening balance) were conceded by the Appellant without costs.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Remarkably, the scientific eligibility of Consoltex's projects was not the central battleground at trial. The DNR's own Science Advisors had conducted a technical review and authored a science report confirming that the representative projects satisfied the statutory definition of SR&ED—conclusions that aligned with the independent expert report filed at trial by the Appellant's textile engineering expert, Dr. Arthur D. Broadbent. Instead, the financial audit division of the DNR's Montreal District Office challenged the quantum of the claimed expenditures on three distinct legal and accounting grounds.

First, the Crown raised a preliminary procedural objection based on an audit-stage settlement agreement. During audit negotiations on January 15, 1992, Consoltex's Vice-President of Finance, Mr. Barry Yager, signed an agreement with DNR assessor Mr. Dennis O'Grady consenting to a formulaic "carve-out" reduction that allowed approximately 44.4% of the claimed SR&ED expenditures across the 1985 to 1988 taxation years. The Crown contended, as a preliminary question, that this signed agreement—which had been offered by Mr. Yager, accepted by Mr. O'Grady, and used as the basis of the reassessments—barred the taxpayer from pursuing its appeals before the Tax Court of Canada.

Second, on the substantive computation of the claims, the Minister advanced the "netting" and "carve-out" theories. Because the experimental fabrics produced during the SR&ED trials were subsequently sold to commercial customers, the Minister contended that the gross SR&ED expenditures must either be reduced by the gross revenue realized from those sales (the "netting" approach) or, alternatively, that the standard manufacturing cost of producing an equivalent volume of commercial fabric must be "carved out" of the section 37 SR&ED expenditure pool and reclassified as ordinary Cost of Goods Sold ("COGS") or inventory under section 9 of the Act.

Third, the Crown challenged the eligibility of raw materials—specifically yarn—and the high yardages woven during experimental trials. The respondent's principal focus was on the amount of fabric produced (Mr. O'Grady was concerned about lengths of 20,000 metres woven in some projects and 52,000 metres in one, on the premise that more material was produced than was needed for development purposes), on the effect of the sales, and on the effect of subparagraph 37(7)(c)(ii) of the Act and section 2900 of the Regulations—including whether yarn transformed into salable cloth could constitute "materials consumed" within the meaning of paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations (the "Regulations") or a current expenditure directly attributable to SR&ED under subparagraph 37(7)(c)(ii) of the Act.
Governing Statutory Framework

The dispute in Consoltex was adjudicated under the pre-1998 statutory architecture of the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Regulations. Subsection 37(1) of the Act permitted a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct expenditures of a current nature made in the year (or carried forward from preceding taxation years after 1973) on SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer. Paragraph 37(7)(b) of the Act provided that "scientific research and experimental development" had the meaning assigned to it by regulation. Subsection 2900(1) of the Regulations defined SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis," categorized into basic research under paragraph 2900(1)(a) (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view), applied research under paragraph 2900(1)(b) (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view), and experimental development under paragraph 2900(1)(c) (use of the results of basic or applied research for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes). Conversely, paragraphs 2900(1)(d) through (j) of the Regulations explicitly excluded activities with respect to market research and sales promotion (d), quality control or routine testing (e), research in the social sciences or the humanities (f), prospecting, exploring, or drilling for or producing minerals, petroleum, or natural gas (g), the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process (h), style changes (i), and routine data collection (j).

To qualify as an eligible SR&ED expenditure in Canada, subparagraph 37(7)(c)(ii) of the Act restricted current expenditures to two statutory streams: clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(A), covering expenditures where all or substantially all (administratively interpreted as 90% or more) of the outlay was attributable to the prosecution of, or the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for, SR&ED in Canada; and clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(B), covering current expenditures directly attributable, as determined by regulation, to the prosecution of, or the provision of premises, facilities or equipment for, SR&ED in Canada. For the purposes of clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(B), subsection 2900(2) of the Regulations prescribed three categories of "directly attributable" expenditures: paragraph 2900(2)(a), the cost of materials consumed in such prosecution; paragraph 2900(2)(b), the portion of salaries, wages, and related benefits paid to employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting such prosecution; and paragraph 2900(2)(c), other expenditures that are directly related to such prosecution and that would not have been incurred had such prosecution not occurred.

In turn, subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the Act governed the entitlement to Investment Tax Credits, authorizing a deduction against Part I tax otherwise payable equal to a specified percentage (20% for Consoltex) of the taxpayer's "qualified expenditure," which subsection 127(9) defined by direct cross-reference to expenditures qualifying under paragraph 37(1)(a) or subparagraph 37(1)(b)(i), excluding prescribed expenditures and, in the case of a corporation, expenditures specified for the purposes of clause 194(2)(a)(ii)(A). Finally, section 9 of the Act governed the general computation of profit from a business—including inventory valuation and Cost of Goods Sold deductions—while subsection 4(4) of the Act operated as a statutory bar prohibiting the double deduction of the same expenditure under more than one provision of the Act.
The Court's Final Holding

Judge Bowman allowed Consoltex's appeals in full with costs (excluding the two conceded issues, for which it was agreed there would be no costs) and referred the assessments back to the Minister for reconsideration and reassessment in accordance with his reasons, which—by agreement of the parties that the result for 1988, argued on the basis of ten representative projects, would govern all the years under appeal—held that the claimed expenditures qualified under section 37 and subsection 127(9). On the preliminary issue, the Court held that the January 15, 1992 settlement agreement was legally unenforceable and did not bar the taxpayer's statutory right of appeal, because, applying the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Cohen (which Judge Bowman followed reluctantly), the Minister lacks the capacity to bind himself to an agreement to assess otherwise than in accordance with the law, and it would be unacceptable for the taxpayer to be bound by an agreement that the Minister remains free to repudiate; accordingly, neither party was bound. On the substantive SR&ED issues, Judge Bowman held that whether an activity constitutes SR&ED must be determined objectively against the criteria of the Act and Regulations, because the disposition of the product does not affect the nature of the activity whereby it is created—wholly irrespective of whether the resulting experimental product is subsequently sold, stored, or scrapped. Furthermore, the Court rejected both the "netting" of sales proceeds and the "carve-out" of standard inventory costs as lacking any statutory foundation in the Act; an expenditure can simultaneously constitute a cost of inventory under section 9 and a qualified SR&ED expenditure under section 37 (subject only to the subsection 4(4) bar against double deduction), and whittling away at SR&ED incentives when experimental trials yield marketable output defeats Parliament's purposive objective of encouraging scientific research in Canada. Finally, the Court confirmed that the cost of raw materials (yarn) necessarily utilized in shop-floor experimental runs qualified as a current SR&ED expenditure under both clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(A) of the Act and paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations.
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures and Statutory Vulnerabilities

A rigorous legal and technical deconstruction of Consoltex requires analyzing two distinct layers of failure: first, the taxpayer's operational, accounting, and audit-governance vulnerabilities that triggered the Minister's disallowance of $5,937,111 in claimed SR&ED expenditures across the 1985–1988 taxation years; and second, the Crown's conceptual and statutory failures at trial, which subsequently prompted Parliament to enact sweeping legislative amendments in 1998 to close the statutory gap exposed by Judge Bowman's ruling.
Procedural and Governance Failure: The January 15, 1992 Audit Compromise

The most acute procedural failure committed by the taxpayer occurred during the audit resolution stage. Following a written submission by Consoltex's external auditors (Price Waterhouse, represented by Mr. Di Palma) on July 10, 1991, and an exchange of memoranda between Mr. O'Grady and the Department's head office in Ottawa that produced no final resolution, Mr. Di Palma (Price Waterhouse), Consoltex's Vice-President of Finance, Mr. Barry Yager, and Ms. Antoinelle Lapolla (listed with Consoltex) met with DNR assessor Mr. Dennis O'Grady in Mr. Yager's office on January 15, 1992. At that meeting the appellant presented Mr. O'Grady with a document setting out its SR&ED expenditures (reproduced as Schedule I to the reasons) and, concerned that the Department might assess using the netting method or carve out 65% of the SR&ED expenditures as cost of sales, Mr. Yager wrote and signed a separate handwritten agreement addressed to Revenue Canada stating: "I agree to the 56% basis for establishing allowable R&D expenditures in taxation years 1985 to 1988". On Mr. O'Grady's copy (Exhibit A-4), 56% was struck out and 55.6% written in and initialed by Mr. Yager; 55.6% was in turn struck out and "*44.4%" substituted in Mr. O'Grady's handwriting, with the notation "confirmed with Barry Yeager [sic] January 15, 1992 at 3:09 p.m." (55.6% being the portion carved out to cost of sales and 44.4% the portion allowed as SR&ED), while Mr. Di Palma's copy (Exhibit A-7) bears neither the 44.4% substitution nor that notation.

body.text: Note: When combined with net allowed SR&ED for Outerwear Fabrics ($385,729), Print Fabrics ($76,176), and direct expenses (for example, salaries of persons engaged exclusively in SR&ED), total allowed 1988 SR&ED expenditures equalled $1,103,788 out of $2,485,829 claimed—yielding an overall allowance ratio of approximately 44.4% (applying the 20% ITC rate produced allowed ITCs of $220,758; the reasons describe this as 44.6% of the amount claimed, although the arithmetic yields 44.4%).

From a tax litigation governance perspective, executing an informal percentage compromise with a field auditor without securing a formal statutory determination—reportedly on the external auditor's advice that the taxpayer had nothing to lose because it could always object, a point on which Judge Bowman expressly declined to make findings (Mr. Yager did not testify) and which he held was not germane—created a severe preliminary jurisdictional hazard. The Crown contended that the agreement barred the appeals, although Judge Bowman held that the question was not one of estoppel in pais. Consoltex escaped this procedural trap because Judge Bowman, considering himself bound by the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Cohen (while expressing disagreement with its rigidity), held that neither party was bound by the agreement; in reaching that conclusion he reviewed Galway v. Minister of National Revenue ([1974] 1 F.C. 600, 74 D.T.C. 6355 (FCA)), Cohen v. The Queen (80 D.T.C. 6250 (FCA)), Smerchanski v. Minister of National Revenue (76 D.T.C. 6247 (SCC)), Canadian Superior Oil Ltd., and Goldstein v. R.

Judge Bowman observed that under the rule established by the Federal Court of Appeal in Galway and Cohen, the Minister of National Revenue is bound by a strict statutory duty under the Act to assess the exact amount of tax payable on the actual facts and the law, and lacks the legal capacity to enter into an extra-statutory compromise agreement—such as the 44.4% allowance formula premised on the carve-out method (which Judge Bowman observed would be as good as any other if the carve-out principle were legally appropriate). Furthermore, estoppel in pais relates to representations of fact and cannot override the law; Judge Bowman held that estoppel had nothing to do with Cohen and had no application in Consoltex. Addressing the apparent doctrinal tension between Smerchanski (where a taxpayer who expressly waived appeal rights to avoid a threatened prosecution was held bound—a case Judge Bowman distinguished because, before him, there was no express waiver of objection or appeal rights, no threat of criminal prosecution and no allegation of undue influence) and Cohen (where the Crown successfully repudiated an assessment agreement that the taxpayer had relied upon to its detriment), Judge Bowman refused to interpret the two cases as creating an asymmetrical, one-way legal regime where the taxpayer is bound by a settlement agreement that the Minister remains free to ignore. If the Minister lacks statutory authority to enter into ultra vires compromise agreements, then no valid contract exists for either party. While Judge Bowman voiced strong policy reservations against a legal regime that undermines principled tax settlements, he reluctantly concluded that under Cohen, neither the Minister nor Consoltex was bound by the January 15, 1992 agreement. Nevertheless, in modern Canadian tax practice—particularly following subsequent jurisprudence affirming principled factual settlements and statutory waivers executed under subsections 165(1.2) and 169(2.2) of the Act—signing an audit settlement without rigorous legal scrutiny can permanently extinguish a taxpayer's right of recourse.
Technical and Operational Vulnerabilities: Shop-Floor Scale and Yardage Justification

A second major source of friction arose from the physical scale of Consoltex's experimental trials and the blurring of operational boundaries between experimental development under paragraph 2900(1)(c) and routine commercial production excluded under paragraph 2900(1)(h) or style changes excluded under paragraph 2900(1)(i). During the audit, the DNR's assessor, Mr. O'Grady, was concerned about some of the lengths of fabric woven—in some cases 20,000 metres and in one 52,000 metres—and the carve-out approach was premised in part on the view that more material was produced than was needed for development purposes. By agreement of the parties, the trial proceeded on the basis of ten representative projects from the 1988 taxation year (five selected by Consoltex and five selected by the Minister), with the outcome governing all five taxation years under appeal.

cells: Fire-Resistant Nomex Project (Development 2169) (Industrial)
Develop a specialized flame-resistant Nomex fabric for oil-drilling personnel satisfying rigid mass-per-unit-area (weight) and thermal protection standards.
Encountered problems with dyeing and with the original warp and filling yarns; wove ~6,000 m using one yarn and about 1,500 m using another.
The dyeing and yarn problems were worked through and the fabric went into production.
Development 2146 (Industrial)
Engineer a reduced-weight ballistic fabric capable of meeting impact-stopping criteria for bulletproof vests.
Executed multi-layer ballistic weaving trials; testing of a 20-layer assembly confirmed bullet-stopping capability but failed the weight-reduction threshold.
Failed the weight-reduction objective; when the fabric went into production, it was sold as protection for hockey players.
Development 5931 (Fashion — DNR Selected)
Enhance surface lustre of an existing fabric architecture by replacing the texturized polyester filling yarn with a more expensive non-textured yarn.
Required engineering a new warp construction and five distinct dobby weave patterns; numerous weaving problems were encountered; 20,000 m were woven and 1,340 m finished.
The development went into production after the numerous weaving problems were worked through.
Development 6123 (Fashion — DNR Selected)
Develop a new blouse fabric using a very fine Japanese filling yarn.

Numerous technical problems were encountered with the weaving (none with the dyeing and finishing); several machine trials, including simultaneous tests on four looms, were needed to establish the correct weaving procedure; 20,000 m woven, with only 404 m finished.
Correct weaving procedure established through the machine trials; the development went into production.
Development 6042 (Fashion — DNR Selected)
Reproduce existing visual patterns utilizing a novel yarn composition and a newly engineered warp construction at reduced yarn density.
Numerous problems were encountered; each incremental mechanical loom adjustment required weaving several hundred metres of cloth to stabilize and evaluate (~15,000 m total).
The development went into production after ~15,000 m of iterative shop-floor experimentation.
Development 2182 (Industrial — DNR Selected)
Reduce the weight of outer-shell fabric for firefighters' suits while keeping the fabric breathable (meeting weight and permeability objectives).
Required special sizing procedures, special loom adjustments, and tests with various types of coating; failed initial tests before succeeding after ~3,000 m.
Initially failed to achieve the weight and permeability objectives but ultimately succeeded; about 3,000 m woven in total.
Development 5110 (Outerwear — DNR Selected)
Determine whether nylon warp yarn exhibiting broken filaments could be salvaged and utilized as filling yarn and warp construction for lining fabrics.
Initial R&D requisition specified only 2,000 m; however, so many problems were encountered that 52,000 m were ultimately produced, much of it substandard.
The project was not successful; the material was ultimately sold for use as liners in sleeping bags.

body.text: The critical evidentiary vulnerability was the high yardage woven—52,000 metres in Development 5110, where only 2,000 metres had initially been requested for R&D purposes, 20,000 metres in Developments 5931 and 6123, and about 15,000 metres in Development 6042. As Judge Bowman analyzed it, the Department's concern about excessive yarn had to rest on one of two hypotheses: that the researchers were incompetent or profligate in their use of yarn, or that they were in collusion with production staff to produce more material than development required so that the cost of the excess would qualify for ITCs. At trial, Consoltex addressed this concern through viva voce and documentary evidence, including the expert report of Dr. Broadbent (which preceded the project descriptions in Exhibit A-1), which explained that large amounts of material may be used before all of the problems are identified and solved, if they are solved, that the seemingly high yardages are particularly noticeable where the experimentation relates to weaving (less material being needed for conversion and finishing tests), and that in Development 6042 several hundred metres of fabric had to be woven between each loom adjustment. Judge Bowman accepted Dr. Broadbent's evidence, finding no evidence that any yardages woven were unnecessary for the experimentation being conducted, and firmly rejecting any premise that researchers were incompetent, profligate, or colluding with production staff to disguise regular production as SR&ED.
Statutory Interpretation and Accounting Failures: "Netting," "Carve-Out," and Raw Materials Consumption vs. Transformation

The third cluster of legal issues centered on how the Act treats raw materials used in SR&ED when those materials are physically incorporated into a product that is later sold. The Crown's position suffered from three fundamental legal defects, yet simultaneously exposed a major tax policy loophole that Parliament moved rapidly to close in 1998.

First, the Crown's primary "netting" theory—which posited that gross SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) must be reduced by revenues generated from selling experimental output—violated fundamental canons of statutory interpretation. As Judge Bowman explained, the word "expenditure" in ordinary parlance means an outlay or something spent; it does not mean "net expenditure after deducting sales proceeds". Where Parliament intended to reduce the section 37 expenditure pool or qualified expenditures under subsection 127(9), it did so through express statutory reductions, such as the deduction under paragraph 37(1)(d) of any government assistance or non-government assistance (as defined in subsection 127(9)) received or receivable in respect of the expenditures; on this point Judge Bowman expressly agreed with the decision of Lamarre Proulx J. in Cultures Laflamme (1984) Inc. Because Parliament chose not to enact a provision offsetting commercial sales proceeds against SR&ED expenditures, reading such a reduction into subsection 37(1) was legally impermissible.

Second, the Crown's alternative "carve-out" theory—which sought to reallocate standard manufacturing costs out of section 37 and into ordinary inventory or Cost of Goods Sold under section 9 whenever experimental fabric was sold—rested on a false premise of mutual exclusivity. While Judge Bowman noted that the carve-out theory had a "certain facile attraction," he demonstrated that it failed upon close statutory analysis. An outlay is not forced into a binary choice between being an SR&ED expenditure under section 37 or a cost of inventory under section 9; rather, an expenditure can simultaneously possess both legal characteristics. Because section 37 is a specific incentive regime designed to encourage scientific research in Canada, whittling away at those provisions whenever experimental output is sold defeats Parliament's legislative object. A taxpayer whose expenditures satisfy the statutory criteria of SR&ED is entitled to claim them in full under section 37 and earn Investment Tax Credits under subsection 127(5), while subsection 4(4) of the Act operates simply to prevent the taxpayer from deducting that same outlay a second time when computing ordinary business profits under section 9.

Third, the dispute exposed a critical drafting tension in the pre-1998 version of Regulation 2900(2) concerning raw materials. Under the pre-1998 text of paragraph 2900(2)(a), directly attributable materials were restricted to the "cost of materials consumed" in the prosecution of SR&ED. Technically, "consumed" implies that a material is destroyed, expended, or rendered virtually valueless during the experiment. Because Consoltex's yarn was woven into fabric that was sold, Judge Bowman himself held that it would put a strained interpretation on the word to say that such yarn was "consumed". Judge Bowman nonetheless resolved this statutory bottleneck by rejecting the view that paragraph 2900(2)(a) is the exclusive route for the cost of materials, and by holding that in textile SR&ED, raw materials such as yarn are obviously a cost of the research, which could not be carried on without them, and therefore qualified under both clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(A) of the Act (as an expenditure all or substantially all of which was attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED) and the catch-all provision in paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations (as "other expenditures that are directly related to such prosecution and that would not have been incurred had such prosecution not occurred").

While Consoltex prevailed completely for its 1985–1988 taxation years, its victory exposed an unintended fiscal asymmetry: a manufacturer could conduct massive shop-floor production runs involving genuine experimental development, claim 100% of the raw material costs for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits, and then sell the resulting inventory for full commercial value—retaining both the tax credit and the commercial profit without any credit clawback. Recognizing that Consoltex effectively invalidated Revenue Canada's administrative "carve-out" practices, the Department of Finance intervened in the February 24, 1998 Federal Budget with two complementary legislative amendments that govern modern Canadian SR&ED practice. First, effective for expenditures incurred after February 23, 1998, paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations was amended to explicitly include both "materials consumed" and "materials transformed" in the prosecution of SR&ED, thereby codifying the initial eligibility of raw materials integrated into experimental output during shop-floor trials. Second, Parliament enacted the ITC recapture regime in subsections 127(27) through 127(36) of the Act specifically to overrule the financial windfall in Consoltex. Under subsection 127(27), where a taxpayer acquires property or transforms materials into property the cost of which was a qualified SR&ED expenditure, and subsequently sells that property or converts it to commercial use, the taxpayer must add back ("recapture") into its Part I tax payable an amount equal to the lesser of the ITC rate applied to the cost of the property or materials and the ITC rate applied to the fair market value or proceeds of disposition of the commercialized output. Concurrently, the CRA abandoned its discredited carve-out formulas around 2000 and introduced Application Policy SR&ED 2002-02R ("Experimental Production and Commercial Production with Experimental Development")—now consolidated into the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy—shifting the administrative inquiry from arbitrary accounting carve-outs to strict technical demarcation between experimental production runs and commercial production with simultaneous experimental development.

Unenforceable if Extra-Statutory: Under Galway and Cohen, the Minister must assess strictly per the Act; a compromise agreement as to the manner of assessment binds neither the Minister nor the taxpayer (a result Judge Bowman reached reluctantly, while agreeing with academic criticism of Cohen and Galway as too rigid).
Principled factual settlements or settlements accompanied by a valid waiver of objection/appeal rights (ITA s. 165(1.2) / s. 169(2.2)) are strictly enforced; arbitrary compromises remain ultra vires.
Definition of SR&ED vs. Commercial Production
ITA s. 37(1), s. 37(7)(b); ITR s. 2900(1)(a)–(c) vs. Exclusions in s. 2900(1)(h) & (i)

Taxpayer conducted R&D on the commercial shop floor without a separate lab. The respondent focused on the sale of fabrics produced in the SR&ED and on the amount of fabric produced, although it was not seriously disputed that the projects involved SR&ED.

Objective Contemporaneous Test: SR&ED eligibility is determined objectively by the systematic investigation and technological uncertainty present during the trial, regardless of whether output is sold, stored, or scrapped.
Formalized into the five-question test in Northwest Hydraulic (98 DTC 1839) and CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy. Commercial sale does not taint underlying valid SR&ED.
Justification of Shop-Floor Trial Scale & Volume

High yardages woven (e.g., 15,000 m to 20,000 m in several projects and 52,000 m in Dev. 5110 after an initial 2,000 m request) raised the assessor's concern that more material was produced than development required.

Technical Necessity Standard: Where there is no evidence that any amounts woven were unnecessary for the experimentation, and credible expert evidence explains that large amounts of material may be used before problems are identified and solved (e.g., several hundred metres between loom adjustments), the full yardage qualifies.
Taxpayers must contemporaneously document why pilot or commercial-scale batch sizes are technically required to test the hypothesis and precisely when technological uncertainty ceases.
Treatment of Commercial Sale Proceeds ("Netting")
Probably the larger part of the experimental fabrics was sold, and total sale proceeds exceeded the SR&ED expenses claimed. Crown argued sales proceeds must be netted against SR&ED expenditures.
Plain Meaning of "Expenditure": "Expenditure" means gross outlay, not net of revenue. Unlike government assistance (s. 37(1)(d)), Parliament enacted no offset for sales proceeds.
Gross expenditures remain eligible under s. 37(1); however, ITA s. 127(27)–(36) now recaptures (claws back) the ITC when SR&ED property or transformed material is sold or converted to commercial use.
Inventory Cost Reallocation ("Carve-Out")

The reassessments applied a "carve-out" formula (computed in Schedule I, presented by the appellant and accepted by the assessor) removing 80% of the net standard production cost of the SR&ED-stage fabric, on an agreed assumption that 80% of that production was sold, from s. 37 into ordinary COGS/inventory under s. 9.

Non-Mutually Exclusive Categories: An outlay can qualify as both a s. 9 inventory cost and a s. 37 SR&ED expenditure. Such expenditures are entitled to the beneficial treatment accorded by section 37, subject only to s. 4(4) preventing double deduction.
CRA abandoned the "carve-out" approach around 2000. However, where experimental development occurs simultaneously alongside a commercial production run, only incremental costs are eligible.
Eligibility of Raw Materials (Yarn)
Yarn costs dominated the claim. The Court itself held that yarn woven into salable cloth was not "materials consumed" under pre-1998 ITR s. 2900(2)(a).

Broad Direct Attribution: Raw materials essential to shop-floor trials qualify under clause 37(7)(c)(ii)(A) ("all or substantially all") and ITR s. 2900(2)(c) ("directly related... would not have been incurred" but for SR&ED).
ITR s. 2900(2)(a) was amended post-Feb 23, 1998 to explicitly cover "materials consumed or materials transformed", paired with s. 127(27) ITC recapture upon sale.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the legal principles of Consoltex—together with its subsequent legislative refinements under Regulation 2900(2)(a), subsections 127(27) to 127(36), and Northwest Hydraulic—into actionable compliance strategies, the following two industry case studies demonstrate step-by-step how Canadian taxpayers must structure shop-floor SR&ED governance, technical documentation, contractual arrangements, cost accounting, and audit dispute protocols.
Case Study 1: Continuous Shop-Floor Experimental Production in Specialty Polymer-Coated Aramid Textiles
Industry Scenario and Audit Pitfalls

Laurentian Technical Fabrics Inc. ("Laurentian"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation ("CCPC") operating an industrial weaving and coating mill in Drummondville, Quebec, undertakes an experimental development project to engineer an ultra-lightweight, arc-flash and flame-resistant para-aramid/modacrylic blended fabric coated with a novel fluoropolymer dispersion for electrical utility linemen. Because the rheological shear behaviour of the coating and the abrasion resistance of the blended warp yarns cannot be replicated on benchtop laboratory equipment, Laurentian conducts its experimental trials directly on its commercial Dornier air-jet looms and industrial knife-over-roll thermal curing range.

Over a 14-month period, Laurentian originally budgets 3,000 linear metres of experimental fabric across three trial runs. However, due to severe filament fibrillation during high-speed air-jet insertion and micro-delamination of the fluoropolymer coating during thermal curing, Laurentian executes 11 iterative shop-floor runs totalling 42,000 linear metres, incurring $680,000 in specialty yarn and chemical feedstock costs and $220,000 in direct engineering and operator labour. Of the 42,000 metres produced, 8,000 metres are scrapped during destructive testing, 24,000 metres of degraded intermediate trials are sold to an industrial distributor as secondary thermal insulation blankets for $190,000, and the final 10,000 metres (where the delamination problem was resolved at metre 35,000) are sold to Laurentian's primary utility customer for $210,000.

Laurentian faces three severe audit pitfalls directly mirroring the vulnerabilities in Consoltex. First, its Enterprise Resource Planning ("ERP") system logged all 42,000 metres under a single production work order (WO-8841) without differentiating where experimental development ended and commercial fulfilment began, replicating the 52,000-metre overrun in Consoltex Development 5110. Second, by continuing the final run from metre 35,000 to metre 42,000 after weaving and curing parameters had stabilized, Laurentian co-mingled 7,000 metres of routine commercial production excluded under paragraph 2900(1)(h) with 35,000 metres of genuine experimental development. Third, Laurentian claimed the entire $680,000 raw material outlay as "materials consumed" without accounting for the post-Consoltex statutory distinction between materials consumed (the 8,000 metres scrapped) and materials transformed (the 34,000 metres sold), prompting the CRA auditor to propose disallowing the entire 42,000-metre run as commercial production or, in the alternative, offering an informal 75% "carve-out" compromise during audit negotiations.
Step 1: Project Governance and Shop-Floor Trial Gatekeeping

To defeat any administrative presumption that commercial production is being disguised as SR&ED, Laurentian must establish a formal Experimental Production Protocol governed by a cross-functional SR&ED Steering Committee comprising the Vice-President of R&D, the Plant Manager, and the Tax Controller. Under this governance framework, open-ended production work orders are strictly prohibited for R&D trials. Instead, every shop-floor trial must be authorized via a discrete Experimental Trial Requisition ("ETR") capped at the exact minimum physical batch size dictated by the equipment's mechanical constraints. Specifically, Laurentian's engineering governance dossier must document that a commercial warp beam requires a minimum of 3,500 metres of continuous yarn to maintain uniform beam tension during slashing and air-jet shedding, and that at least 400 metres must pass through the knife-over-roll thermal curing oven per parameter change to reach thermal equilibrium—mirroring the type of evidentiary foundation provided by Dr. Broadbent's expert report in Consoltex. Furthermore, the Steering Committee must establish objective, quantitative "freeze-gate" termination criteria before the loom starts, specifying a target warp breakage rate of ≤ 2 stops per 100,000 picks and hydrostatic coating adhesion of ≥ 25 N/5 cm after 50 thermal cycles. The instant the quality assurance laboratory verifies that the fabric at metre 35,000 has achieved these metrics, the ETR automatically terminates, and the remaining 7,000 metres on the warp beam are transferred in the ERP system to a standard commercial production work order (PROD-8841B).
Step 2: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation and Experimentation Tracking

To satisfy the objective evidentiary standard required by Judge Bowman in Consoltex and the five-part judicial test articulated in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1839), Laurentian must implement granular, batch-linked technical logging that distinguishes technological uncertainty from routine machine troubleshooting. The technical project records must first document why standard textile engineering knowledge and supplier datasheets could not predict the tribo-electric and mechanical interaction between the para-aramid/modacrylic yarn hairiness, the polyvinyl alcohol sizing bath viscosity, and the fluoropolymer curing temperature. Across the first 35,000 metres (encompassing ETR-01 through ETR-11), engineers must maintain a digital loom and coating log tying every yardage interval to a specific hypothesis and variable manipulation. For example, the log for metres 12,000 to 15,500 (ETR-04) must record the specific hypothesis that increasing slashing bath solid content from 8.5% to 11.2% and reducing air-jet main nozzle pressure from 4.8 bar to 3.9 bar would eliminate modacrylic fibril accumulation in the reed tunnel, followed by the quantitative experimental observation that weft stops decreased by 62% while residual sizing polymers triggered fluoropolymer blistering at a 190 °C curing profile. This unbroken chain of contemporaneous evidence proves that every single metre woven up to metre 35,000 was strictly required for systematic investigation by means of experiment or analysis under subsection 2900(1).
Step 3: Accounting Segregation, Materials Transformed, and ITC Recapture Optimization

Rather than claiming a monolithic $680,000 material pool and risking a punitive audit disallowance, Laurentian must restructure its General Ledger and Form T661 claim to align precisely with Regulation 2900(2)(a), section 37, subsection 4(4), and subsection 127(27). First, to comply with the subsection 4(4) prohibition against double deductions, Laurentian must transfer the $566,667 in yarn and chemical costs and $183,333 in direct labour attributable to the 35,000 metres of valid experimental production out of ordinary section 9 Cost of Goods Sold and into a dedicated section 37 SR&ED Expenditure Pool account, while leaving the costs of the final 7,000 commercial metres ($113,333 in materials and $36,667 in labour) strictly within ordinary commercial inventory under section 9.

Second, within the eligible 35,000-metre experimental pool, Laurentian must bifurcate its raw material costs under the post-1998 wording of paragraph 2900(2)(a). The $129,524 in raw materials attributable to the 8,000 metres of destructively tested and scrapped fabric must be classified as Materials Consumed under Regulation 2900(2)(a). Because these materials were destroyed and rendered valueless, they attract full federal and Quebec R&D tax credits with zero ITC recapture under subsection 127(27). Conversely, the $437,143 in raw materials attributable to the 27,000 metres of experimental fabric that were subsequently sold (comprising the 24,000 metres of degraded seconds and the 3,000 metres of successful trial output woven between metre 32,000 and metre 35,000) must be classified as Materials Transformed under Regulation 2900(2)(a). When the 24,000 metres of seconds (carrying an original material cost of $388,571) are sold as secondary insulation blankets for $190,000, subsection 127(27) triggers ITC recapture based on the lesser of the original material cost ($388,571) and the proceeds of disposition ($190,000). Because the degraded fabric sold for less than half of its raw material cost, Laurentian permanently retains the ITC generated on the $198,571 unrecovered material cost differential, retains 100% of the ITCs on all direct SR&ED labour ($183,333) and overhead, and deducts 100% of the $750,000 expenditure under subsection 37(1).
Step 4: Audit Dispute and Settlement Governance

To prevent a repeat of the January 15, 1992 compromise trap in Consoltex, Laurentian must enact a corporate governance resolution prohibiting the Vice-President of Finance or Controller from signing any CRA audit proposal letter, Schedule I adjustment sheet, or statutory waiver of objection rights without formal written clearance from tax litigation counsel. When presented with the auditor's proposed 75% "carve-out," Laurentian's tax counsel must submit a formal legal memorandum citing Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen (97 D.T.C. 724) and the CRA's own SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, demonstrating that accounting "carve-outs" and "netting" were declared legally baseless by the Tax Court of Canada in 1997 and abandoned by the CRA in 2000. Counsel will establish that the commercial sale of experimental runs is policed exclusively through the statutory recapture formula in subsection 127(27)—which Laurentian has already self-assessed on its 27,000 metres of sold trial output—leaving zero legal basis to reduce the section 37 pool or disallow the labour and unrecovered material credits.
Case Study 2: Custom Metallurgic Casting Trials and Subcontractor Commercial Supply Contracts
Industry Scenario and Audit Pitfalls

Northern Alloy Foundry Corp. ("Northern"), an advanced metallurgical engineering firm in Hamilton, Ontario, enters into a $2.4 million commercial supply contract with a Canadian mining company ("MineCo") to deliver 12 ultra-high-chromium white-iron slurry pump casings capable of withstanding extreme abrasive-corrosive tailing environments. Because no existing alloy composition or sand-mould directional solidification protocol can prevent carbide micro-cracking in castings exceeding 4,500 kg, Northern must conduct extensive experimental foundry trials on its commercial induction furnaces and pouring floor.

Northern pours 9 full-scale experimental castings ($110,000 in virgin ferro-alloy and nadir sand mould costs per pour; $990,000 total material cost) before resolving the thermal gradient cracking challenge. Pours 1 through 4 crack severely during heat treatment and are remelted as internal foundry scrap; Pours 5 through 7 exhibit minor subsurface porosity that fails MineCo's primary pressure specification, but MineCo agrees in a contract amendment to purchase them at a 77.5% discount from the $200,000 contract unit price ($45,000 each; $135,000 total) for low-pressure auxiliary water lines; Pours 8 and 9 succeed completely and are delivered as the first 2 of the 12 contracted commercial units (generating $400,000 in contract revenue), followed by 10 standard commercial pours (Pours 10 to 19). During the CRA audit, Northern's Chief Financial Officer orally agrees with the CRA reviewer to drop Pours 5 through 9 from the SR&ED claim in exchange for the auditor rapidly approving Pours 1 through 4, and signs an informal adjustment sheet.

Northern confronts three interlocking legal pitfalls arising from Consoltex and related Canadian jurisprudence. First, because the overarching contract with MineCo was drafted as a single lump-sum supply agreement without separating R&D risk from commercial unit delivery, the CRA auditor characterizes the customer payments as "contract payments" for SR&ED performed on behalf of a Canadian resident under subsection 127(9) (which, through the reduction of qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18), strips Northern of its ITCs, as litigated in Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 D.T.C. 713, citing Consoltex) or, alternatively, treats all delivered pours as routine commercial production excluded under paragraph 2900(1)(h). Second, the auditor applies a Consoltex-style "netting/carve-out" rationale to Pours 5 through 9, asserting that because Pours 5–7 and Pours 8–9 were delivered to MineCo for commercial revenue, their underlying costs cannot constitute SR&ED. Third, the CFO's execution of the auditor's adjustment sheet threatens to forfeit $550,000 in valid material costs and associated labour on Pours 5 through 9.
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring to Prevent "Contract Payment" Taint and Isolate Experimental Risk

To ensure that customer revenues from MineCo do not disqualify Northern's SR&ED claim under the "contract payment" rules of subsection 127(9) or taint the experimental pours as routine commercial production, Northern must restructure its commercial contracting architecture. The primary supply agreement with MineCo must be drafted strictly as a fixed-price commercial contract for the sale of 12 compliant hardware units meeting performance specification SPEC-400, containing an explicit recital that Northern is not covenanted or obligated to perform SR&ED on MineCo's behalf, that Northern bears 100% of the financial risk of metallurgical development, and that all foreground intellectual property (including alloy recipes, gating geometries, and thermal treatment curves) vests exclusively in Northern. Furthermore, when Pours 5 through 7 fail primary ultrasonic inspection, Northern must not amend the core deliverable schedule of the supply agreement; instead, Northern and MineCo must execute a standalone Salvage Material Bill of Sale. That Bill of Sale must explicitly recite that Pours 5 through 7 were generated during internal experimental solidification trials, failed SPEC-400 technological thresholds, and are being liquidated on an "as-is, where-is" salvage basis for $45,000 per unit—directly paralleling Consoltex's sale, for use as sleeping bag liners, of the fabric produced in the unsuccessful Development 5110 (and, by analogy, its sale as protection for hockey players of the Development 2146 ballistic fabric, which failed its weight-reduction objective, once that fabric went into production).
Step 2: Technical Documentation of Pour-by-Pour Experimental Methodology

To prove that Pours 1 through 9 constituted a single, continuous systematic investigation under subsection 2900(1), Northern must compile a comprehensive metallurgical experimentation dossier bridging the gap between computer simulation and shop-floor foundry physics. The technical narrative must establish why finite-element solidification modelling could not accurately predict primary M₇C₃ carbide precipitation and internal shrinkage porosity across the 350 mm wall-thickness transitions of a 4,500 kg casting. Across Pours 1 through 9, Northern must maintain sequential metallurgical laboratory records demonstrating that Pours 8 and 9 were not "first-article commercial production," but rather the culminating experimental verification runs testing a modified vanadium-titanium micro-alloying addition and a cryogenic quench cycle formulated specifically after Pours 5 through 7 exhibited subsurface porosity. Under Judge Bowman's holding in Consoltex, whether Pours 5 through 9 met the objective criteria of the Act and Regulations is determined objectively by the nature of the activity whereby the castings were created—wholly unaffected by the subsequent sale of Pours 5–7 as salvage or Pours 8–9 as compliant commercial units. Conversely, Pours 10 through 19, which were poured after technological uncertainty was resolved and metallurgical parameters were frozen at the conclusion of Pour 9, must be excluded entirely from the SR&ED claim as commercial production under paragraph 2900(1)(h).
Step 3: Nuanced Cost Tracking — Internal Remelting (Scrap) vs. Commercial Disposition

Northern must structure its cost accounting across the 9 experimental pours to capture maximum ITCs while properly applying the post-Consoltex recapture rules under subsection 127(27). For each $110,000 pour, Northern must separate the cost of expendable nadir sand moulds, cores, and melting fluxes ($40,000 per pour), which are physically destroyed during pouring and shakeout, from the virgin ferro-chromium alloy charge ($70,000 per pour). Across all 9 experimental pours, the $360,000 expended on destroyed sand moulds and melting fluxes ($40,000 × 9) constitutes Materials Consumed under Regulation 2900(2)(a), earning permanent ITCs with zero recapture under subsection 127(27), even on Pours 5 through 9 that were sold to MineCo.

For the $630,000 in metal alloy integrated into the castings ($70,000 × 9), Northern must classify the outlay as Materials Transformed under Regulation 2900(2)(a) and apply three distinct subsection 127(27) recapture treatments based on the disposition of each batch. For Pours 1 through 4 ($280,000 alloy cost), which cracked and were remelted in Northern's induction furnace for subsequent pours, remelting converts the transformed alloy back to commercial raw material inventory at its bulk foundry scrap value ($18,000 per casting, or $72,000 total); thus, subsection 127(27) recaptures ITCs only on the $72,000 scrap value, permanently preserving the ITCs on the remaining $208,000 unrecovered alloy cost. For Pours 5 through 7 ($210,000 alloy cost), which were liquidated as salvage for $135,000 total, subsection 127(27) recapture is capped at the $135,000 proceeds of disposition, preserving the ITCs on the $75,000 unrecovered alloy cost differential. For Pours 8 and 9 ($140,000 alloy cost), which were delivered as full-price commercial units for $400,000, the ITC on the $140,000 transformed alloy is recaptured in full upon delivery (capped at original cost of $140,000), while 100% of Northern's metallurgical engineering salaries, foundry technician labour, non-destructive ultrasonic testing, and furnace energy costs across all 9 pours remain fully eligible for section 37 deductions and section 127 ITCs without any reduction or carve-out.
Step 4: Repudiation of the Unprincipled Audit Compromise and Notice of Objection Strategy

To remediate the CFO's execution of the auditor's informal adjustment sheet dropping Pours 5 through 9, Northern's tax litigation counsel must immediately inspect the document to verify that it does not contain a formal statutory waiver of objection and appeal rights compliant with subsection 165(1.2) or subsection 169(2.2) of the Act. Because the document is merely an informal audit agreement sheet parallel to the handwritten agreement signed by Mr. Yager (distinct from the Schedule I computation presented to the assessor) in Consoltex, Northern must file a formal Notice of Objection under subsection 165(1) within 90 days of the Notice of Reassessment. In its submissions to the CRA Appeals Division, Northern must rely directly on Judge Bowman's holding in Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen (97 D.T.C. 724), supported by Galway v. Minister of National Revenue and Cohen v. The Queen, to establish that an informal audit compromise whereby a taxpayer forfeits statutorily eligible SR&ED pours (Pours 5 through 9) on the legally erroneous premise that sold output cannot qualify as SR&ED is contrary to the Income Tax Act and completely non-binding on both the Minister and the taxpayer.

cells: Trial Volume & Batch Scale Control
Open-ended shop-floor runs (42,000 m fabric / 19 castings) blurring experimental development with commercial production.
Discrete Experimental Trial Requisitions (ETRs) tied to equipment physics and hard quantitative exit gates.
ITA s. 37(1); ITR s. 2900(1)(c) vs. s. 2900(1)(h); Consoltex; Northwest Hydraulic.
Material Cost Classification
Lumping all raw materials into a single bucket vulnerable to complete disallowance when trial output is sold.
Granular split between Materials Consumed (scrapped cloth, expendable sand moulds/fluxes) and Materials Transformed (sold cloth/castings).
ITA s. 37(7)(c)(ii)(A)/(B); Post-1998 ITR s. 2900(2)(a) & (c); Consoltex.
Revenue & Inventory Accounting
Exposure to auditor "netting" or "carve-out" formulas stripping 55%–80% of total R&D costs into ordinary COGS.
Transfer of eligible trial costs from s. 9 COGS to s. 37 pool (per s. 4(4)); isolation of ITC clawback strictly to transformed materials via s. 127(27).
Customer Contract Architecture
Lump-sum developmental supply contracts risking "contract payment" ITC denial or routine commercial characterization.
Fixed-price commercial hardware contracts with IP retention, paired with separate "as-is" salvage bills of sale for substandard trial lots.
ITA s. 127(9) ("contract payment"); Consoltex; Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen.
Audit Settlement Governance

Corporate officers signing informal percentage compromises with CRA field assessors without legal review (in Consoltex, reportedly on the external auditor's advice that the taxpayer could still object).
Mandatory legal review bylaw; rejection of extra-statutory carve-outs; preservation of formal Notice of Objection rights.
ITA s. 152(4), s. 165(1), s. 169; Consoltex; Galway & Cohen.

body.text: 5. Synthesis and Strategic Conclusions for Canadian Tax Practitioners

The legacy of Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen in Canadian tax law is twofold. First, at the macro-interpretive level, Judge Bowman cemented the principle that section 37 of the Income Tax Act and Regulation 2900 are fiscal incentive provisions enacted to encourage scientific research in Canada, which should be interpreted in a manner that encourages such research and that refuses to penalize industrial taxpayers merely because their systematic experimentation occurs on a commercial shop floor or yields salable by-products. Subsequent SR&ED decisions in Canada—most notably Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 D.T.C. 1839), Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen (99 D.T.C. 713), and LGL Ltd. v. The Queen (99 D.T.C. 675)—reflect the purposive approach of Consoltex to the SR&ED incentive provisions.

Second, at the practical compliance level, Consoltex serves as a permanent cautionary lesson regarding the dynamic interplay between judicial victories and legislative counter-measures. While Judge Bowman struck down the Minister's extra-statutory "netting" and "carve-out" theories and confirmed the non-binding nature of unprincipled audit settlements, Parliament's enactment of the subsection 127(27) ITC recapture rules and the "materials transformed" amendments to Regulation 2900(2)(a) in 1998 permanently codified how commercialized experimental output is taxed. Consequently, Canadian corporate taxpayers conducting shop-floor experimental development must combine the evidentiary rigour demonstrated by Dr. Broadbent's trial analysis in Consoltex—establishing that the volumes of experimental output were necessary for the experimentation being conducted—with precise accounting segregation between materials consumed (which remain permanently exempt from recapture) and materials transformed (which are subject to subsection 127(27) recapture capped at commercial proceeds), thereby securing the full statutory benefit of the SR&ED regime without exposing the enterprise to audit disallowances or defective settlement agreements.
